Incumbent Andre Carson is running with roughly $1 million raised; Republican Patrick McAuley reports no fundraising

model.rationale: The seat's deep Democratic lean, Carson's incumbency and large financial edge over a challenger with no reported fundraising, and markets pricing his win near 97% all point to a safe hold. With no polling available, the margin estimate leans on fundamentals, but nothing in the evidence suggests the winner is in doubt.
model.watch: With no polling in the race, an unexpected scandal or a surge in split-ticket voting could narrow the margin, though an upset remains highly unlikely.
notes: No expert rater lists this race; treated as safe for the party holding the seat.
No usable general-election polls; forecast rests on fundamentals and expert ratings.

overview:
Andre Carson, the Democratic incumbent, seeks another term in this Indianapolis-based House district, which leans Democratic by roughly twenty points in partisan terms. He enters the general election with about one million dollars raised and more than six hundred thousand dollars on hand, while Republican nominee Patrick McAuley reports no fundraising figures and Libertarian James Sceniak also appears on the ballot. No public general-election polls are available, and no expert raters have ranked the race.

Prediction markets on Kalshi and Polymarket both price a Carson win at about ninety-seven percent. The district's strong Democratic lean, Carson's incumbency and financial edge, and the absence of any competitive signals point to a comfortable hold. The real uncertainty is the size of the margin rather than the identity of the winner, with thin data leaving room for wider error than in well-surveyed races.
